doc.title: Chico Hamilton interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 30, 2000

title: Leading by developing talent; Dolphy, Lloyd and Coryell
summary: A leader needs patience and fortitude; he kept Dolphy, Charles Lloyd and Larry Coryell despite pressure to fire them.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: Yeah. You’re playing the room, right? That’s great. He also said something — oh he had a nice quote about you. He said, “Chico to me is in a sense like Duke Ellington. He plays his music using any player, any group of instruments. It doesn’t matter what it is he puts his own stamp on it.”

That’s true. That’s true. You know, being a band leader, or a leader of a group, it’s more than just having a name or creating a name or building a name. It’s being able to — knowing when to, how to present something. Knowing — I have an innate sense about well knowing talent, hearing talent, and seeing talent. And I know, see it takes two things, two very important things to reach a stage where you can make music, and that’s patience and fortitude. This I learned very early, in my early youth. So I had the patience to watch a talent develop. And since I’m in the driver’s seat, since I’m there keeping time for him, I can guide them. I can play to their weakness and help them become strong. So knowing

that whatever talent that they might have, there’s always a resentment, a tremendous resentment when someone is different. I’ve been considered, okay I’m an innovator, I know that. Whether that’s good or bad or indifferent, but it’s a very lonely life, because you’re constantly — I’m past the stage of trying to please. I don’t please anybody. I play music for music’s sake. There should be no substitute for not playing your best, playing whatever you play. You play your best. And this is my whole thing, my whole being. Whatever I do — I might sound good, bad or indifferent, hey but I’m doing my best. So whenever you’re different it’s going to be ten to one it’s not going to dig you. For an old colloquial expression “dig” means like or dislike. But knowing or feeling hey, man, nobody — like they wanted me to fire Eric Dolphy. They wanted me to fire Charles Lloyd. Larry Coryell. People like that. I said later for that. Straight ahead, you know? And what happened? These guys turned out to be young geniuses.
